episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Working Lands & Industry
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Working Lands & Industry.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is it fair to help the people who are already helping?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Millar Western to indefinitely curtail operations at Quesnel River Pulp mill and All-Ways Travels earns Williams Lake business honour, shares journey through uncertainty, plus 10 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Should forestry money and restart priority go first to the mill operator that kept its crew through lean years, or to newcomers with new plans, and how should conflicting federal and Nation review processes be reconciled? Topics include: Federal forestry funding timing and Bill C-39 fast-track review, Tŝilhqot'in National Government impact assessment framework and its limits, Millar Western mill idle status, effluent system, and restart uncertainty, Competing claims of existing operators versus newcomers, woodlot owners, and Nation-owned ventures, Training for displaced workers and Quesnel council engagement with First Nations.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Agricultural Research Alliance

discussion.central_question: Should forestry money and restart priority go first to the mill operator that kept its crew through lean years, or to newcomers with new plans, and how should conflicting federal and Nation review processes be reconciled?
discussion.riley_position: Nation-set impact assessment criteria, like the Tŝilhqot'in framework, offer a readable, dated standard that can guide a restart and reduce uncertainty, and the operator who stayed through lean years has skills worth prioritizing, though training for the displaced workforce should be required.
riley_key_evidence: The Tŝilhqot'in National Government's impact assessment framework was developed over five years with community members, elders, and knowledge holders, and was released November 9th.
Ottawa says major projects wait five years or more for federal decisions, which Bill C-39 aims to coordinate.
Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation, a Nation-owned joint venture operating through multiple fire seasons, shows Nation-led resource work in practice.
discussion.casey_position: Federal money and fast-track rules favour existing operators and risk sequencing problems, while newcomers, smaller owners, Nation-owned ventures, and displaced workers lack written conditions and a seat at the table; the Nation framework does not bind Ottawa or apply to Quesnel.
casey_key_evidence: The AFN calls Bill C-39 fundamentally flawed and wants it withdrawn; West Coast Environmental Law warned of a dismantling of environmental law.
The COFI statement asks for funding to maintain, modernize, and develop existing operations, without naming newcomers, smaller owners, or Nation-owned ventures.
Millar Western's letter commits only to keeping the effluent system running for twelve months with no restart date, and no budget line exists for training in year five.
discussion.resolution: They did not resolve the core question; they agreed the framework is a useful template to watch, the rules still being drafted are decisive, and the open issue is who will inform Quesnel workers about the status of the mill in the meantime.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: What does Bill C-39 (Building Canada Strong Act) actually change in federal project assessment, and how contested is it?

Findings: Bill C-39 is a government bill in the 45th Parliament's first session. Part 1, "Build Canada Now," overhauls federal environmental and project assessment by amending the Impact Assessment Act, the Canadian Energy Regulator Act, and the Building Canada Act. Law-firm analyses (Gowling, McMillan, Blakes, Cassels) say the government's rationale is that major projects routinely wait five years or more for all federal decisions, while the US, UK, and Australia have streamlined their processes. Specific changes include making the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission responsible for impact assessments of nuclear and uranium projects, and coordinating impact assessments with other federal reviews and federal consultation with Indigenous groups. Critics are sharp. The AFN has called the bill "fundamentally flawed" and asked for its withdrawal. West Coast Environmental Law told a committee it "will bring in a dismantling of environmental law." Critics also warn the bill could let Ottawa grant permits for preliminary construction before the Impact Assessment Agency finishes its review, and that it reshapes Indigenous consultation for mining, oil and gas, and infrastructure projects. Indigenous Climate Action wants UNDRIP and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) written in as binding. Ottawa says projects will be built faster without lowering standards. The Narwhal reports that consultation feedback showed "widespread agreement that reform should not come at the expense of environmental protection or Indigenous Rights." It is still before a special committee and the Senate, so its final form is not settled.

Suggested angle: Riley can argue that five-year federal approval timelines are a real cost to workers and to First Nations seeking economic partnerships, and that a single coordinated review is better than the current patchwork. Casey can press on the sequencing risk, the permit-before-review provision, and whether a "coordinated" consultation process actually discharges the Crown's duty to consult. The Tŝilhqot'in Nation's framework is the sharpest test of this: Riley can point to it as a model of Indigenous-led review that could fit into a faster system, and Casey can ask whether a nation building its own parallel review is evidence that the federal process is not trusted to meet Indigenous rights.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the $6.5 billion federal forestry commitment in Budget 2026 meet the needs of B.C.'s forest sector?

Findings: The federal government says Canada's forest sector faces combined US tariffs and duties of around 35 percent. It will receive $6.5 billion over six years, starting in 2027-28, to improve productivity and competitiveness. The funding was announced in Budget 2026 on November 5, 2026. The BC Council of Forest Industries (COFI), through president and CEO Kim Haakstad, welcomed the money as coming at a "critical time" for workers, businesses, and communities. COFI also said more action is needed to make a considerable difference. Details of how the provinces will divide the money were not yet known at the time of reporting. Coverage notes the funding comes amid heavy US tariffs and mill closures in B.C.

Suggested angle: Casey can frame this as a deferred response: the money starts in 2027-28 and is spread over six years, while mills are closing now, and the allocation hasn't been defined. Riley can counter that a long, predictable productivity investment is what mills need to modernize and compete, and that the industry's own welcome signals it is a real commitment. Together they can ask what "productivity" means for a rural B.C. town: retooling mills, or keeping a sawmill open long enough for a workforce to stay in place.

roundup.opening_frame: A news day where Cariboo mill and budget news sits next to farm stories from around the world, all about who carries the risk when the ground shifts under working industries.

stories.point: Millar Western will indefinitely curtail the Quesnel River Pulp mill, citing market conditions and uncertain economic fibre supply, and will keep the effluent system running for twelve months while it winds down the rest for a possible restart.
All-Ways Travel won the Chamber's Ken Wilson Business of the Year award after owner MJ Vigeant kept it open through the pandemic to help residents make essential trips.
The Quesnel Community Foundation has a $50,000 challenge running to Dec. 15, with an anonymous donor matching what the community gives.

The 2026 federal budget sets aside $6.5 billion over six years for forest-sector transformation, on top of $2.9 billion announced since August 2025, for fibre supply, modernizing facilities and higher-value products, while projecting a $62.3 billion deficit. B.C. leaders and Canadian Forest Owners welcomed it, and the owners want private forests included in the fibre supply plan.
Quesnel's new mayor and council were sworn in at a packed ceremony, with Lhtako Dene and Nazko First Nation leaders speaking about working together on the city's difficult times.
More than a dozen holiday markets are running across the South Cariboo this winter, and the 100 Mile House Christmas Craft Fair on Nov. 14 is the last of its kind, with a second one on Dec. 12.

The Interlakes volunteer fire department bought a new squad truck with money from a community society's fundraising and large donations, on top of the Cariboo Regional District tax funding it already gets.
The USDA is moving nearly $4 million to ten Kansas meat processors to expand local processing options for livestock producers, as part of a $57.4 million round covering 147 awards.
Small Farm Canada's guide says root crops are dependable for small farms and that planting dates vary by region and should be treated as a starting point.
Bird flu was found in 40 Washington dairy herds between Oct. 7 and Oct. 30, mostly in Yakima County, and a county resident exposed to infected cattle died Nov. 1.

Dairy technology is spreading: a New Zealand AI monitoring system now covers 145,000 cows, a Canadian firm reports 9% transport savings, and a Mid Canterbury farmer's lame-cow flags fell from 400 to 30 over three seasons.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both this story and the next are about who controls farm data once it is collected, so we move to Sweden's farmer council.

stories.point: Swedish farm-data platforms are linking records, crop-protection information and field logs, and Agronod has formed a farmer council whose member says use should stay voluntary.

Spain ordered olive mills to hold back 12% of output without payment for storage, after growers said prices of about €3 a kilogram were well under production costs near €5, while bottlers plan to challenge the order.
Farms in New Zealand, Poland and Vietnam are adding tourism, seed processing and intercropping for income, and one New Zealand grower warns diversification is not an easy way to make money.

Guinea banned illegal artisanal gold mining in Siguiri and expelled foreign miners, sending workers into Mali and Burkina Faso, where hospitals treated injured returnees and Burkina Faso says it got no advance notice.
Cleanfarms will run seven free collection events in Prince Edward Island from Nov. 16 to 27 for old pesticides and livestock medications.

roundup.handoff: Ottawa's forestry money is promised, the Quesnel mill is already idled over fibre supply, and the question left hanging is who sets the rules for projects on the land in between.

deep_dive.central_question: With Ottawa promising $6.5 billion for forestry over six years from 2027/28 while fast-tracking project review through Bill C-39, does the Tŝilhqot'in Nation's new impact assessment framework give working Cariboo industries a clearer route for investment, or one more gate between a curtailed mill town and its restart?
deep_dive.riley_holds: A Nation-designed review process with published values and criteria gives capital and workers a known path, and a project that passes it is more likely to last than one rushed through.
deep_dive.casey_holds: Fast-track timelines and funding timelines are being set elsewhere, so the mill workers and towns who carry the risk wait on an unresolved clash of processes while the owners keep the margin.

beats.claim: The Tŝilhqot'in framework turns the Nation's say over projects into a published process with stated criteria, rather than a reaction to each proposal.
beats.evidence: Tŝilhqot'in National Government release of Nov 9: the Impact Assessment Framework sets the Nation's process, values, principles and criteria for projects affecting nen (land and resources), deni (people) and Aboriginal title and rights, and was developed over five years of engagement with community members, elders, knowledge holders and leaders.
beats.pushback: Casey: a framework sets expectations, but the release is timed against Bill C-39, the Build Canada Strong Act, which is being rushed through to fast-track major project review. The material does not say how Ottawa's process will treat the Nation's one, so a published process is not the same as a binding one.
beats.leads_to_next: If the two processes may collide, the question is what a project proponent or a mill owner is actually waiting on, which brings in the money and its timing.

beats.claim: The federal forestry money and the mill closures are on different clocks, so what working towns need now is certainty about rules, not only cash later.
beats.evidence: My Cariboo Now (covered in Sunday's roundup): COFI's Kim Haakstad welcomed the $6.5 billion but said more action is needed, and the funding is delivered over six years starting 2027/28. Williams Lake Tribune/Observer: Millar Western curtailed Quesnel River Pulp indefinitely over market conditions and uncertain economic fibre supply, setting it up for a possible restart.
beats.pushback: Riley: that gap is the argument for clear review rules. A restart or a modernization that has to pass a known Nation process can plan around it, whereas a fast-tracked approval that is later challenged leaves the same mill idle. Casey answers that nothing in the material shows any mill or program has been tied to the framework yet.
beats.leads_to_next: If the money is aimed at keeping existing operations going, the next question is who it reaches and who bears the risk if it doesn't work.

beats.claim: Federal funding language favours existing operators and owners, so the risk stays with workers and towns while the investment decisions sit with companies.
beats.evidence: COFI statement: Haakstad wants program details that support capital investments to maintain existing operations, modernize facilities and develop new products. Canadian Forest Owners (Canadian Forest Industries, budget story from roundup): wants private forests counted in the fibre supply solution. Williams Lake Tribune: the budget projects a $62.3 billion deficit this year.
beats.pushback: Riley: modernization money for existing mills is how jobs are kept, and the Nation's criteria can attach conditions about what a working town gains. Casey replies that the COFI statement itself says program details are still to be worked out, so conditions that favour communities are not yet written anywhere.
beats.leads_to_next: Both hosts need the case to land somewhere specific, so we turn to who in the Cariboo would actually be in that room.

beats.claim: In the Cariboo, a Nation's review framework and a mill town's restart hopes meet in the same neighbourhood, and neither is currently guaranteed a place in the other's timeline.
beats.evidence: Quesnel Cariboo Observer: at the council swearing-in, Lhtako Dene Chief Clifford Lebrun and Nazko Chief Leah Stump spoke of working together with the city and the Cariboo Regional District on city issues in a difficult time. Tŝilhqot'in National Government is based in Williams Lake and its framework covers Tŝilhqot'in nen. The Millar Western letter covers the Quesnel mill.
beats.pushback: Casey: the Tŝilhqot'in framework applies to Tŝilhqot'in territory, not to the Quesnel mill, so the link is about the model and not a direct fix, and Quesnel's fibre problem is not shown to be about review rules at all. Riley concedes the point and keeps only the narrower claim that Nation-set criteria are the best available route to a restart that holds.
beats.leads_to_next: With the link narrowed, what remains is who answers to a mill town when two processes disagree, which is the landing.

deep_dive.cariboo_beat: The fourth beat: it ties the Tŝilhqot'in framework and the Lhtako Dene and Nazko chiefs' remarks at Quesnel's council swearing-in to the idled Quesnel River Pulp mill, while being clear the framework covers Tŝilhqot'in territory.
deep_dive.landing: Held open: when a Nation's own impact assessment and a federal fast-track both claim to review the same kind of project, whose decision should promised forestry capital wait on, and who is responsible for telling a mill town like Quesnel where things stand in the meantime.
